chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Wartime shortage of musicians and the decline of big bands
summary: Many musicians joined the armed forces; McRae's brother Bob led a Navy band; travel limits and rising small bands undermined big bands.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: All right. Now, during the war period, was there a shortage of musicians -- a

noticeable shortage of musicians --
Yeah.
-- or, were the musicians because the big bands -- out of work (inaudible)?
No. It was a shortage of musicians, because a lot of musicians were going in the Army and Navy.
Remember I was telling you that Artie was in Hawaii or somewhere? And my brother, Bob, went in the Navy -- lieutenant or something, you know.
And he was the band conductor over there. He built a big band down at Pier 39, the west side -- the pier down there.
And they had this little Army and Navy base there. And my brother's in the Navy there. He went in the Navy and he built this big Navy band. Had all these top musicians.
Took a lot of musicians from New York. got All the top musicians (inaudible) in the Navy. Chief and all this stuff. Petty Officer (inaudible).
And they all went -- (inaudible) played all these dances and everything -- canteens and things
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

for the Navy. When they come in, the soldiers have these parties and things. That's all they played. They'd go all over. And eventually, Artie Shaw was coming back, so he went out to take Artie Shaw's place. And he stayed out there until the war was over.

Even though you were with Louie at the time, and also, of course, earlier in the war with Hampton, and the war's winding down and you're going out your own -- you did notice -- you were aware, that is, of the fact that the band seemed to be -- something was changing. That there weren't as many orchestras active as they were except the top orchestras.

Yes, you're right there. Even at the time that I was with Duke -- with Cab -- Duke was having a very bad time, (inaudible) trying to hold the band together. Remember, because just before Joe Glaser after those years, took him over (inaudible) I think later -- forty or fifty something -- '47, something like that, when
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Glaser took the band.
You know, Johnny Hodges and all the boys had left the band, you know. The big bands were just going down.
That's when the small bands were coming in -- they wasn't getting too much work for the big bands, and things like that.
And that was one of the years during that time -- leading up to that time when Louie Jordon and all the bands were coming out.
Louie had went into his thing, you know, and all those small bands were coming up and they were doing real good.
And it was a shortage of musicians, because a lot of musicians had went to war. A lot of the musicians joined the Navy and a lot of them was doing the U, you know, travelling for the Army, and they were just doing shows overseas, and travelling like that.
Because I told you when '45 -- when we went to California with Louie, there was a command performance, we saw a lot of musicians. All that band --

was all the top musicians in that band out there. And you could imagine all the different bands the Army had. And the band doing the other travelling for the Army -- it was a real shortage of musicians. It wasn't too many big dances, because it was too -- I tell you one thing that's really stopped bands was during the war, because the bands couldn't move around. They had no transportation. The only thing that kept us going during the ware years was Joe Glaser had worked out a deal for us to play these Army and Navy hospitals and benefits and things.
Transportation was covered by the armed services.
